projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Mike Rebich was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: This is the oral history of World War II veteran, Mike Rebich. Mr. Rebich served in the US Army with the 143rd AAA Gun Battalion, Battery C. He served in the European Theater and his highest rank was PFC. I am Tom Swope and this interview was recorded at Mr. Rebich's home in Euclid, Ohio on August 28th, 2003. Mike was 79 at the time of this recording.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Where were you living in 1941?

sp.speaker: Mike Rebich
sp.p: I was living on 160 Collingwood, that is Cleveland.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Do you have specific memories of December 7th, 1941?

sp.speaker: Mike Rebich
sp.p: Yes, I lived at that time in Fairport, Ohio, which is about thirty miles or so from Cleveland and of course I was a teenager at that time and I remember that day quite well.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Do you remember hearing the news?

sp.speaker: Mike Rebich
sp.p: Yes, uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What did you think when you heard about that?

sp.speaker: Mike Rebich
sp.p: Well, we're at war. There wasn't much you could say.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Were you still in school at that time?

sp.speaker: Mike Rebich
sp.p: No, I wasn't. I just came out of school and I started working. I had family to support, my sisters and my mom. My dad died, so I had to go to work.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Now in your situation, I suppose, were you tempted at all to go out and sign up for the draft or sign up for the service?

sp.speaker: Mike Rebich
sp.p: No, I didn't since, of course, my family depended upon me and of course, I moved to Cleveland. I stayed with friends until I got a job here and then I got my mom and my sisters, so we all lived together here in Cleveland. But I didn't sign up because I knew I was going to be drafted.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So you would be drafted even though -- Wouldn't you have a deferment as a supporter of the family?

sp.speaker: Mike Rebich
sp.p: I got a deferment for about six months and then after that, why, I didn't want any more deferment. I thought I might as well get it over with and go in.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So when were you drafted then?

sp.speaker: Mike Rebich
sp.p: It was August 10th, 1943.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So what was that like when you went into the service and were thrown in with guys from all over the country?

sp.speaker: Mike Rebich
sp.p: Well, it was quite excitable. We knew we had a job to do and the job was going to be done. So, we had to do the best we can. So our outfit was made up from fellows from West Virginia, Ohio, Pennsylvania, Kentucky, you know. And then others came while we were in California and Camp Hahn, which is across from March Field. Then others came from all over the country, two, three, four, five, whatever. So, we made a good outfit.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: That had to be the first time though you were exposed to guys from all over the country?

sp.speaker: Mike Rebich
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Wasn't that a little strange?

sp.speaker: Mike Rebich
sp.p: Yeah. Not really. It wasn't for me. I am outgoing person and I accepted everybody for what they are and we realized that there was a war on. We had to do something about it and that was it.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Were you assigned to the 143rd right out of basic training?

sp.speaker: Mike Rebich
sp.p: We were assigned to 143rd, right, we were at Fort Hayes, Columbus Ohio. And we were all shipped out to Camp Hahn, so we must have been assigned right there at Columbus to 143rd.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So that was even before you took any basic training?

sp.speaker: Mike Rebich
sp.p: Yeah. Right, definitely.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Because Fort Hayes is --

sp.speaker: Mike Rebich
sp.p: We started and we came out, 143rd. In fact, for about six months we were in Military Police. We didn't have enough points to get out, so they shipped the old fellows home that had points, and of course, we were short on some points and so we were put into Military Police.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: This is at the end of the war?

sp.speaker: Mike Rebich
sp.p: That was, yeah, right. And the strange thing is we were attached to the Ninth Air Force, so I went as I told you into the Military Police. So I just decided I was going to go and see someone at the Ninth Air Force Headquarters and talk to them, how many points I had. So, I told him and everything else and they looked up my record and they said well, you got enough points to go home. So me and my big mouth, I went back and told my fellow MPs that I am going home, that I had enough points. And the whole mess of them went out to the Ninth Air Force. They says we were with Mr. Rebich, or Private Mr. Rebich, and we have enough points too, so they said we're going home, too. So they called me up on the phone and they says you don't have enough points. We made a mistake. So we served for six months in Military Police. But it wasn't bad, I didn't mind it. It was a different experience.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Now, backtracking a bit, what can you tell me about your training?

sp.speaker: Mike Rebich
sp.p: The training was hard but very interesting, very interesting. We went on the 30 miles hike and we went on short hikes and we learned to live with it.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Anything unusual or out of the ordinary happen during your training time?

sp.speaker: Mike Rebich
sp.p: Yes, we were, got our march orders at night. You dug the gun in and everything else and maybe an hour later they tell you march orders. In other words, dig out got the gun now and move to another location. So one time we moved, we must have been about 12:00, 1:00 o'clock in the morning to Muron (phonetic), which is Edwards Air Force Base now, right outside of that because we were with the Air Force, assigned to the Air Force. And so we went out there and we started digging in and about 3:00 o'clock they sent everybody to bed, and of course each gun had their man on the forward in case they get a march order, so you wake everybody up. So they put me on the phone and being tired, digging in for three, four hours, putting the gun in, I fell asleep. And they got a march order and everybody is up, putting their guns together, and my gun crew was still sleeping on account of me. So I got a week of KP for the punishment. So that was about the only exciting thing that happened to me during the basic training.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What was your job with the gun unit?

sp.speaker: Mike Rebich
sp.p: I was a loader on the 90 millimeter. Yeah, I was putting the shells in.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So you were actually loading the shells?

sp.speaker: Mike Rebich
sp.p: Oh, yes, I put the shells in the gun. And the faster you were, the better your gun crew was because you really had to, those shells weighed about 40-some pounds and you have to be fast. Slim and slender, that is what I was and so they picked me for that job.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Because it was kind of cramped quarters, you needed to fit?

sp.speaker: Mike Rebich
sp.p: You had about twelve inches between the breech coming back on recoil and another instrument where the fellow was tracking. So you didn't have much room so you had to be slim. So, that was my job.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Any other stories from your training?

sp.speaker: Mike Rebich
sp.p: Well, right now, I really don't. I suppose you got all kind of stories.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh. I just one wondered if anything comes to mind.

sp.speaker: Mike Rebich
sp.p: But one other story, of course, we had to take a 30-mile hike. And I had a friend that lived in the east side of Cleveland and he was a little older fellow, so he was ready to clunk out. And so I took my pack, his pack, his rifle, so he could make it and carried it for him. And finally, we took a break and then we started back, 15 miles one way and then 15 back to the camp. And I was able to, I was used to walking, so it didn't really bother me all that much, but there was a lot of dropouts so they had a truck picking them up. Of course, they had to take that course over again, but I thank the Lord I was able to make it and I didn't have to take it over again.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So when did you ship overseas, approximately?

sp.speaker: Mike Rebich
sp.p: We shipped in '44. I don't remember. I got it marked down somewheres. We shipped in '44 for I think, let's see, it was, I think it was in August. Yeah, in August.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What was that crossing like?

sp.speaker: Mike Rebich
sp.p: Crossing was, we had one of the biggest convoys they tell me that has ever crossed Atlantic. There was ships all over. And they put me on, it was a British ship and they put me on the orlican guns for the aircraft, since we were anti-aircraft. So they put me on that, on the watch, four hours on and 10 hours off or whatever it was, you know. So that was quite scary because we had quite a few alerts of German subs lurking around. But I should say thank God that we never, none of our ships were sunk to my knowledge. But the only close call we had at night was there was a terrible fog and one of the ships, you could almost touch it from the back end, how close it was. That scared me. It could have rammed us and that English ship, it was so old I understand it sunk on its own when it reached the channel. So, that was quite an exciting trip.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did you land in England first?

sp.speaker: Mike Rebich
sp.p: Yes, we landed in England and we were there about three weeks. And then we went across the channel. And the front lines were five to ten miles in already. So we were in the back protecting the rear against the German paratroopers and stuff like that. And we were there for number of weeks, then they sent us to Paris. And we were in Paris for about six months or something like that guarding Paris against German planes. And of course, we didn't have no German planes coming over Paris, but we had V-2 rockets, which scared the daylights out of us. Just exploded. You didn't hear them, you didn't see them. They just exploded.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: These are the V-2s?

sp.speaker: Mike Rebich
sp.p: V-2s, yeah and V-1. Of course, you could see those things and we were in Belgium when the Germans let loose on those and they drove our outfit bananas because they were all over the place and you couldn't shoot because you tipped them, then they'd come right down at you. We had a cook out there, he was a master sergeant. He was our chief cook. And he was going bananas because they were falling all round us. That was in Liege, Belgium. And it was quite an experience with that. Then the Battle of the Bulge broke out.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Where were you set up when the Battle of the Bulge broke out?

sp.speaker: Mike Rebich
sp.p: We were in Liege and in fact, we moved to in Namur, another little town from Liege, and that is where we were not too far from where the Germans were. We made it. So they lent us to First Army. General Hodges was in charge of First Army. And they put us, Captain Kent of course, led us out to a village, Stumont Village. It was a small town and we were Gun One. And as we were following him in a Jeep he told us where to go. It was across the road and our gun, believe it or not, it was 19 degrees so, but our gun stuck in the mud. It was terrible. We didn't get our gun down. And you know, I could see now and I thank the Lord that it was, because that was the first place the Germans attacked, Gun One. But we had one fellow that ran to our gun, he wasn't even our gun, and he mounted a .50 caliber machine gun on an M4 tractor and he was shooting and he got killed. He was the only one that I know of that got killed. And after our gun was destroyed, they put us fellows and infantry to guard Gun Two. And then while I was by Gun Two, they told me to go and take a .50 caliber machine gun off the truck. And as I was about to take it off, a gentleman, his name was Philips, DP Philips, whatever, he was from was West Virginia. He was in charge of that .50 caliber machine gun, that was his gun and he said let me do it, I know more about this. So as he went up there to take the machine gun off, it went off accidentally and cut his leg off. And I was supposed to do that a few seconds before and he pushed me out of the way and as he was taking it out, he didn't have his safety on and he was rolling on the ground there. And good thing we had some good medics. They took him and they saved his leg, they shipped him in the States and they saved his leg. They sewed his leg on. And I heard in a meeting out there in Columbus, a reunion meeting, one of the fellows that lives nearby says that he was doing fine. That he was limping, but he got his own leg. Yeah. So that was quite a scary time for me.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Now when your gun was stuck in the mud, it was just stuck, were you able to use it then at that point?

sp.speaker: Mike Rebich
sp.p: They, from what I understand they had to blow it up. The strange thing here is now another thing. No other gun hit any mud but Gun One. Now, mind you, I was a loader on that gun. Then as we were out protecting Gun Two, Germans were coming over the hill, I was standing next to Lieutenant McGuire and next to him was First Sergeant. They were shooting at the Germans. I had mud in front of me and my rifle fell right into the mud. Like unseen hand hit that rifle and it was loaded with mud. And I was wondering should I shoot or not, so I asked the lieutenant. I said what should I do? I said should I take a chance to shoot? He said if you want to have your head blown out, go on, pull the trigger, but get back. He was mad at me. I wasn't -- I didn't do it deliberately. Like unseen hand hit that thing. It stung my hand how, from the force and the gun went into the mud. No one else hit mud. In fact, I tell you how hard that ground was around there. I was trying to dig a fox hole, I couldn't even dig a fox hole. It was frozen. And yet I had gun -- mud in front of me and the big gun got stuck, 90 millimeter. So you figure out what happened. Strange thing. And by the time I got back to clean my gun, why, we started retreating and I jumped on the Jeep, there was a Jeep, must have had about five, six guys in there already. So they just, he didn't stop, he was just slowing down and I leaped and they dragged me down on the Jeep and we went and I never had a chance to face the enemy after that.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Captain Kent told me about that action at Stumont where they got the tanks. Were you involved in that, where they caught those tanks in an ambush?

sp.speaker: Mike Rebich
sp.p: Oh, yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: You were there?

sp.speaker: Mike Rebich
sp.p: There was one tank, the Gun Two was sitting against the station, train station like, you know. We would have had the best view if we would have had our guns set down because we were right there, right facing them as they were maneuvering there, but since we were knocked out out there and stuck in the mud. So Gun Two, we went by Gun Two and they seen this tank coming down making a turn and they shot it. They went to shoot it from the tank and let the bullet shell go underneath the tank and explode and set the thing ablaze because those things were monsters. Things were bouncing off of them like a BB gun. And then we had Durago and Seamon from the gun, they took bazookas, one of the guys from the 30th Infantry Division, he said who can handle a bazooka? We all had training, but we never really were all that familiar with it. So these two gentlemen volunteered and they went out there and they knocked one tank off. They had to shoot at the treads to blow the treads out. So the first tank and the second tank were keeping the other tanks from going that were trying to, Germans were trying to push the tanks over the hill because it was a mountainous range out there, but they couldn't. And then we finally seen British, I don't remember what armored division it was, British coming up towards the front. And we were glad to see them coming from with the tanks, because what could we do, 140 guys with rifles against -- they were heading, they had mortars, they were bombarding us all over the place. But I am surprised that more guys didn't get killed. They had a ring around us practically and they were shooting us from all directions. So we just, we lost more than one guy. There was two guys that I know of that were killed there. So, they got one listed, but there was at least two guys, maybe even more. So it was a little rough.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: This was Battery C of the 143rd?

sp.speaker: Mike Rebich
sp.p: Battery C, yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Any other memories from the bulge?

sp.speaker: Mike Rebich
sp.p: Well, we were stationed, we were put into place out there and on top of the hill were the Germans and their V-2, V-1 rockets. They were launching them from the bottom of this little, it was a little slope, slopey hill and the bottom of this hill was the V-2 rockets taking off, and of course, we couldn't do anything about it. So that was a little scary because and then we had this home that was right on the road. There was no cover or anything, somebody must have lived there before we came there and we were sitting ducks in their home and were fortunate that the Germans didn't blow us up. So, we had some scary moments, but after all the Lord was good to 143rd. We lost men, but it wasn't a disaster.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So what came next after the Bulge for you?

sp.speaker: Mike Rebich
sp.p: Well, after that, the war was almost, we were sent to Bonn, Germany and we were there when the war ended. So they told us, well, from now on they said we're going to Japan so we started to sort of, preparing to go to Japan and the word came about the atomic bomb and then of course, that was cancelled out.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Do you remember any particular celebrations on VE day or VJ day?

sp.speaker: Mike Rebich
sp.p: Yes, we got quite pie-eyed right after the Battle of the Bulge was over. Boy, that was, everybody celebrated. But after VE day, everybody was happy that they didn't have to go to Japan, because you know they predicted that a million American soldiers would have been dead invading Japan. So, we were very fortunate that that was cut short.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Was the plan for you to be transferred to the infantry?

sp.speaker: Mike Rebich
sp.p: No, we probably would have went as a unit, as 143rd unit, but we don't know what they would have used us for. Anti-tank guns, anti-aircraft, artillery or whatever. So we didn't know.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What happened then -- We touched on this a little earlier. What happened after VJ day? You ended up as Military Police?

sp.speaker: Mike Rebich
sp.p: Yes, we went to into Military Police for about six months until we, then they told us we got enough -- See they couldn't replace us. The outfit, they formed a new military outfit and they, we had to guard the Ninth Air Force Headquarters out there. So this is where they needed the police and they couldn't let everybody go home and they wouldn't have had no Military Police out there. But my job was the dirtiest. I was guarding coal piles and the last day, believe it or not, it was a scary one. They came to me said you got to go and guard a C-47 crash-landed about 30 miles from camp. I said why me, I told myself but I went. And now of course they only gave you a .45. You had no carbines or anything like that. So I had a .45 and they took me to guard throughout the night from 7:00 o'clock to 7:00 o'clock in the morning. And I went, and of course, I went in a plane and no one was around. It was maybe about 15 miles or so from the village, nearest village. And here I seen about a dozen Germans coming with buckets to siphon the gas and I was there alone and the only thing I could tell them when they came there they wanted gas, I understood a little German, I told them to, that they had to get out of there. I said "Verschwinde von hier" they had to get out of there. And they just stood there, so they were talking among themselves and I had no choice but to pull my gun out and I only had nine rounds in the gun and there was 12 of them. I said I am going to get killed, but before I get killed I am going to take some of them with me. But again, you know, prayer is a mighty thing in the hands of a sinner and I just said that silent prayer to myself. Did you know that they turned around and left? And 7:00 o'clock they came and picked me up, took me back. He said get ready, we're going home and we left. But that was a last scary night I had.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So you came home soon after that?

sp.speaker: Mike Rebich
sp.p: Oh, yeah, yeah, yeah. We had a quite exciting trip, too. We came on a liberty ship and we hit a storm. And of course, 90 percent of them, the guys were sick, sea sick, but they put me in the kitchen. Of course, that didn't bother me, crossing the ocean, because I was born in Europe and I crossed the ocean once before. So, there is another thing I want to mention to you. When I went to California I wanted to find out if I was a citizen. Someone told me yes, you are, through your parents. Someone else came along and said no, you are not, you're going to have to get your citizenship. So when they got ready to go overseas, I refused to go. I said you give me my citizenship or else I'm not going. You can't force me. That is the law. So they said okay. About a week later, I went to San Bernardino and I got my citizenship papers. So, that was, Army is a wonderful life and I would recommend it for all our young men. But, of course, today with dope and everything that they got there, you have to be very careful. But I never heard of dope out there at that time. You know, we had a nice bunch of fellows and everybody got along and we went, had our passes and everything else. Wonderful time.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So when you were in the Army of Occupation, other than that incident at the C-47, did you have much contact with the German citizens?

sp.speaker: Mike Rebich
sp.p: No, not really. We seen the prisoners, you know, in trucks and stuff like that, but we never had any real close. We were always in the back, guarding the Air Force, airports, stuff like that. Planes taking off, make sure that they were more or less safe from the German aircraft. And one time, I don't know whether it's true, but they, we got our alert and a big English Lancaster bomber, it was like our B-17, somebody mentioned, well, yous guys done a good job, you shot a Lancaster down. So, I don't know whether we did or not, but that was what the rumor was.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: How about in Belgium or France? Did you have much contact with any of the local people there?

sp.speaker: Mike Rebich
sp.p: Oh, yeah, quite often. Yeah, yeah, they used to -- Here is another thing, I don't know maybe it was some of the other fellows told you. Our guys were trying to out-smart the Frenchmen and the Belgium fellows so they would come and buy cigarettes, carton of cigarettes. It was forty dollars a carton. So our guys would take horse manure, cut the pack off, take the cigarettes and stuff them with horse manure, but the top they left full packs and they were selling them to the Frenchmen. So you know what the Frenchmen used to do to our guys? They urinate in the bottle and corked it and selling that for cognac. That is the truth.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did any of the guys drink it?

sp.speaker: Mike Rebich
sp.p: Some, I heard some guys tasted it and they knew that it was urine but I didn't touch that. When I heard the story that was going around I said no way, I'm not.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: But you were only in England for you said about three weeks. Did you have any contact with the English people?

sp.speaker: Mike Rebich
sp.p: Yes. We had dances and stuff like that. But we had a hard time, some of us, understanding English people. Their boat was a little something unusual and we had to put the best of it, try to use sign language and everything else to understand them, really. But it wasn't bad, of course, three weeks, that wasn't all that bad. We weren't allowed to fraternize with people. We were restricted and until, then after that we were put on the boats and shipped across the channel.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Was there much souvenir collecting when you were over there?

sp.speaker: Mike Rebich
sp.p: Yes, there was quite a few. And a lot of fellows saw the Dutch wooden shoes, buying those and shipping them home. And I had done a stupid thing, I bought an accordion out there, a button box, an accordion in Germany. And I packed it up ready to send it and some guy, he was my gun sergeant at one time, he lived in Baltimore, I sold it to him for twenty dollars. And I only bought some, brought a gun home and a sword and bayonets, German bayonets and stuff like that. But most of the souvenirs I sent home through mail.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Captain Kent told me at one point the Headquarters, the Battery, wanted your Battery to share souvenirs with them?

sp.speaker: Mike Rebich
sp.p: I didn't hear about that, but I wouldn't be surprised, because we were the ones that were --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: You were out there.

sp.speaker: Mike Rebich
sp.p: Yeah, we were in the town where one of the biggest, where they used to make watches, Schwenningen out there. And then they had in schools and everything else, they had little small lakes, making parts for watches and everything else. We were so tempted to steal one of those things. But of course, what would I do with it?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Do you have memories of mail call, getting letters or packages from home?

sp.speaker: Mike Rebich
sp.p: Oh, yeah, uh-huh. One package my mom sent me for one Christmas I got for the next Christmas, but the cookies were still good. The package was all beat up. But I got, that was the longest about a year, yeah, but usually it took maybe three, four months.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did you write much home?

sp.speaker: Mike Rebich
sp.p: Yes, I did, of course, yeah, whenever you found time.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What kinds of thing would you write about?

sp.speaker: Mike Rebich
sp.p: Well, there wasn't much you could write because they sensor your mail and they would just clip those things out. In fact, I wrote in Croatian and believe it or not they had Croatian sensors out there took that scissors and clipped some of that stuff out. So we tried not to say too much about what was going on. In fact, my mom got a letter from me stating "Delayed in Enemy Action." So the Germans, when that gun that, we had a tractor there and we had a our equipment up there, so the Germans must have took all of our equipment out of there. And the letter was in their hands and then when the allies attacked, the British and Americans, then they recaptured our stuff and our mail was in there and so they sent it home through the regular channels. And when my mom got it, she was worried about me and it says Delayed in Enemy Action, but I was all right.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: When you finally got home, what was your reunion with your family like?

sp.speaker: Mike Rebich
sp.p: Well, it was good to see them. It was good to see them. It was quite an experience. And one thing the fellows that went there came home together. Most of the buddies that I shoved around after there, you know, in the neighborhood, so we had a wonderful time together.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did you have close buddies overseas?

sp.speaker: Mike Rebich
sp.p: Oh, yeah, definitely. One was my best man when we got married and we chummed around after we got out of service, in fact, two guys. We were always together.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did you lose any close buddies over there or were you lucky?

sp.speaker: Mike Rebich
sp.p: I was lucky. Like I said we lost couple guys that I know of. And --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: When you think about your experiences over there, does any other particularly vivid memory come to mind?

sp.speaker: Mike Rebich
sp.p: You know, there is so much when you start thinking. Right now my mind is sort of blank but we had some, they took us guys and they took us to see this Berchtesgaden, Hitler's in the Bavarian hills. That was something strange to see, you know, how they build up practically this hide-out for Hitler and his staff out there, and he was -- It was really something to see. It was all bombed out and everything else.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So were you able to tour the --

sp.speaker: Mike Rebich
sp.p: Yeah, I went through there. Then we went and seen Dachau where they, that was something terrible to see. They had rooms out there where they threw the bodies. The blood, you could see the stained walls about maybe four or five feet high. That was terrible to see where they shot them and buried them and some of them they just threw them in the ovens. They had one oven and then they built two more ovens. Yeah, in fact, I have got some pictures on that. And then when we were in Germany we took a trip to Chamonix. That is his Mont Blanc out there where, it was a beautiful scenery out there. That is where they ski at summertime, Mont Blanc out there. So they had this trolley car that take you up there and you look down you see cars look like match boxes. So that was a beautiful experience for me.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Anything else?

sp.speaker: Mike Rebich
sp.p: Right now, I don't have anything.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: That is why we keep talking, if something else comes to mind. Do you think we have covered it?

sp.speaker: Mike Rebich
sp.p: Pretty close.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Okay. [End of Interview]
